title: Stuart Broad Admits Jadeja's Trademark Sword Celebration 'Used to Annoy' Him
excerpt: The retired England pace legend said he couldn't understand why Jadeja would wave his bat after milestones, adding to a long history of English frustration with the Indian all-rounder's iconic ritual.
body:
• Former England fast bowler Stuart Broad admitted that Ravindra Jadeja's sword celebration "used to annoy" him during matches, asking "What's the guy waving bat for?"
  • Jadeja tormented England in the 2025 Anderson-Tendulkar Trophy, scoring 516 runs including five half-centuries and one century in the drawn 2-2 series
  • The celebration is rooted in Rajput warrior tradition called 'talwaar baazi,' first performed during a Test at Lord's in 2014
  • Broad is not the first England player to react — James Anderson famously mimicked the celebration during the 2024 Rajkot Test

Retired England fast bowler Stuart Broad has admitted that Ravindra Jadeja's trademark sword celebration used to get under his skin during their on-field battles.

"It used to annoy me a bit," Broad said, questioning the purpose of the ritual. "What's the guy waving bat for?"

The candid remarks add another chapter to what has become one of cricket's most entertaining subplots — the English frustration with Jadeja's celebratory bat-twirling, a gesture the Indian all-rounder performs every time he reaches a milestone in international cricket.

A Celebration Rooted in Warrior Tradition

Jadeja's celebration is far from a random flourish. The 37-year-old from Jamnagar, Gujarat, has explained its origins lie in Rajput culture, a tradition he calls 'talwaar baazi' — sword fighting performed during festivals and special occasions.

"It has got to do with a tradition that we have among the Rajpoots. During festivals and special occasions, we have professional sword-fighters perform with a sword in each hand. I only had one bat with me so I did it with one hand."

— Ravindra Jadeja

Jadeja first performed the celebration after scoring a half-century at Lord's during the 2014 Test series against England, and it has since become one of the most recognizable rituals in world cricket.

England's Long History With the Sword

Broad is not the first England cricketer to take issue with the celebration. James Anderson memorably mimicked Jadeja's sword twirl behind his back during the third Test at Rajkot in February 2024, after the Indian all-rounder completed his fourth Test century. Anderson and Jadeja had a fraught history dating back to a heated altercation during the 2014 Lord's Test, where both camps accused the other of physical and verbal abuse.

Former England captain Michael Vaughan also weighed in during the COVID-19 lockdown in 2020, when Jadeja posted a video of himself wielding a real sword. Rather than complimenting his skills, Vaughan quipped: "Your grass needs a mow, Rockstar."

Jadeja Tormented England in 2025 Series

Broad's irritation may have been compounded by Jadeja's devastating form against England in the 2025 Anderson-Tendulkar Trophy, where the left-hander amassed 516 runs across the drawn 2-2 series — including five half-centuries and one century. In the fourth Test at Old Trafford, Jadeja scored an unbeaten 107 and, in a twist, skipped his trademark sword, instead performing a Pushpa-style celebration while captain Shubman Gill urged him from the dressing room to bring out the sword.

During that same series, Broad himself criticized Jadeja's slow batting approach during the second Test at Edgbaston. "I can't understand this at all," Broad said on commentary. "Jadeja's almost playing like India are behind the game here. He should be pushing this scoreboard on."

The Numbers Behind the Sword

Jadeja has scored 41 half-centuries across 373 international appearances, each one typically accompanied by the celebration. Former Australia pacer Brett Lee, while praising Jadeja's fitness and predicting he would reach 100 Test caps, jokingly warned that the only injury risk he faces is "doing a rotator cuff with his celebration."

At 37, Jadeja continues to be a force in Tests and ODIs for India, having retired from T20Is after the 2024 World Cup triumph. His sword celebration, love it or hate it, remains an indelible part of modern cricket.
nri_angle: Jadeja's celebration is rooted in Rajput warrior tradition, and the India-England cricket rivalry is followed passionately by the Indian diaspora worldwide.
